prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reach a fractional frequency uncertainty of about 10^-18

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep optical lattice clocks as my preferred single-part prize for Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The central point is a physical principle, not a better instrument: at the magic wavelength the light shift of the two clock levels is the same, so thousands of atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime with no motional or trap shift. That is a new way of controlling neutral atoms, and it is different in kind from the frequency comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012). Katori proposed the idea and made the first lattice clocks, and Ye's group brought accuracy and many-body coherence to about 10^-18. JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE have reproduced and cross-compared such clocks, and this is the independent agreement I trust. The strongest argument I can offer, answering the doubt that this is only a tool, is that the lattice clock resolves the relativistic redshift across about a millimetre, which is a direct observation of gravity acting on a quantum system. The credit is also the cleanest on the shortlist: two names, with no painful cut.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is that the fundamental-physics output so far consists of limits and consistency checks, and the redefinition of the second has not happened. Colleagues who prefer a result that revealed a new state or phenomenon (Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Olsson) will see this as an excellent refinement of an honoured toolbox. B006 has wider ballot support and about twenty years of confirmation across platforms, and I accept that if the committee values breadth of support and conceptual reach over cleanness of credit, B006 is a defensible choice, though its third seat and its relation to the 2016 prize are unresolved. A two-name clock prize also leaves out other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde and SYRTE, and the Yb groups), and I cannot settle priority from what I have.

responses.point: Eriksson asks whether a pending redefinition of the second is a reason to wait or to act, and would be comfortable with B047 in a later cycle because the physical discovery lies in a measurement technology whose payoff has not arrived.
responses.response: My answer is that the redefinition is not a precondition. The Nobel citation should rest on what has been shown, and that is a new scheme (magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms) and a reproduced accuracy of 10^-18, verified by comparisons between laboratories. If we wait for the redefinition we make the prize depend on a metrological committee's schedule, not on the physics. I do agree that twisted bilayer graphene delivers new quantum states now, and I understand why he prefers it. But the pairing mechanism, the sample variability and the Cao and Dean questions are still open, and eight years is short for the kind of independent confirmation I weigh most. That keeps B017 outside my top choices for this year, while I would not call the physics unimportant.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair and a B047 supporter, asks whether the many-body Fermi-degenerate clock results alone make Ye's credit distinct from the comb prize, or whether the redefinition of the second is the real test. He also notes that B006 has the widest ballot support.
responses.response: The comb prize honoured a way of counting optical cycles, and it gave us the ruler. The lattice clock changes what the atoms do: a quantum degenerate gas in a lattice, with spin-exchange interactions controlled so that the clock is not limited by the usual quantum projection noise. That is a many-body quantum system used as a sensor, and it is Ye's distinct contribution. So the distinction rests on the physics, not on the redefinition. I accept his point that B047 has narrower support than B006. I do not treat a support count as a scientific argument, but I will weigh how well a credit can be defended, and here B047 is stronger.

responses.point: Danielsson regards the clocks as an instrument rather than a discovery until the second is redefined or a signal is seen, and ranks B047 seventh. He supports B006 for Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, with a prediction that nature confirmed.
responses.response: I take the instrument objection seriously, and I want the citation to answer it. A millimetre-scale redshift measured inside a single atomic cloud is a result about nature that was not accessible before, and a limit on drifting constants at this level excludes theories. That is information, even if it is a null result. On B006, I accept that it is the better-confirmed case on many platforms and I would not oppose it. But the discovery in the topological case is spread over theory, 2D transport and 3D ARPES, and a three-name cut separates people whose work is inseparable. I cannot judge that attribution as well as the condensed-matter members, so I defer to them there, and I keep B006 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Olsson moved to B006 after reading the opening ballots, insisting that the Mele and Hasan allocation not be settled just because ballots converge, and that the clock be tested against the 2005 and 2012 prizes. She has an institutional contact with Katori's university (Tokyo).
responses.response: I share her view that the committee should not choose a trio because ballots happen to converge, and that applies to my own B047 pair as well. I tested it by asking whether Katori and Ye each hold a role without which the lattice clock would not exist: the first, the idea and the first strontium lattice clocks; the second, the accuracy records and many-body control. I think the answer is yes. I also take her disclosure of ties to Tokyo as relevant for B047, and I suggest the committee note it, though I see no sign that it affects her scientific judgement.

responses.point: Mehlig proposes Kane, Mele and Molenkamp for B006, with a citation naming the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation in HgTe. He asks the experimentalists whether the 3D ARPES work can be fitted in without exceeding three names.
responses.response: I agree that his framing, a citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and the HgTe measurement, is the honest way to handle the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit, and it is the same trio I proposed in the opening round. If the committee goes to B006, I would support that version over one that stretches to cover the 3D case with a fourth, uncredited group. I am not an expert on the ARPES side, so I cannot say if the 3D discovery can fit within three names. It does not change my own first choice, but it makes B006 my main alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct discovery, not a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether other lattice-clock pioneers (SYRTE, the Yb groups) have a claim that two names would leave out; I have not verified priority.
Whether the third seat in B006 is settled (Mele or Hasan), because if it is, B006 may have a stronger case than I credit.
I have not verified the most recent published uncertainty records for these clocks or the schedule for redefining the second.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows no personal or institutional connection to Katori or Ye or their groups, and no collaboration with them. I collaborate closely with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate), the Lund attosecond group and Ursula Keller's group at ETH, which bears on attosecond candidates and not on B047, B006 or B038. I note the disclosures of Kroll, Olsson and Pearce, and Johansson's invitation to discount B038, and I take them into account. I have no new conflict to add.
